transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-02-12 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marco Silva (Redwood SRE); Dana Park (Acme Head of ML), Omar Reyes (Eng Manager), Sofia Lin (PM)

Summary (auto): Technical review of embedding dims, batching, and reranking latency/cost. Agreed pilot and next steps.

[00:00] Jordan (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this pretty technical, priya is going to run through the perf numbers and then we can talk infra and next steps
[00:32] Priya (SE): awesome, yeah thanks jordan. so high level, acme's ask is low-latency online reranking for search results, target p95 around 75ms end-to-end when reranking topK=10, and cost needs to stay under our estimate. you sent the dataset sample, correct dana?
[01:02] Dana (Acme): yes sent a 200k row sample, mostly product titles and descriptions, and we expect production to be about 10M vectors; but online traffic for rerank is ~500 qps peak with bursts to 1k qps
[01:20] Priya (SE): perfect. so two-stage pattern we usually recommend: stage 1 dense retrieval via vector index (FAISS/HNSW) using precomputed embeddings, stage 2 neural cross-encoder rerank for topK. that lets you keep most embedding lookups cheap and only pay for cross-encoder compute on small topK
[01:45] Omar (Acme): quick Q: for embeddings do you recommend 1536 dims or smaller? storage costs of 10M x 1536 are a concern
[02:01] Priya (SE): right — tradeoffs. 768 dims often give 90-95% of quality for many product/text tasks, 1536 gives better recall/nearest-neighbor fidelity esp for subtle semantic distinctions. 2048+ rarely required unless you have very fine-grained taxonomy. storage math: 10M * 1536 * 4 bytes = ~61GB raw (float32). with int8/4 quantization you can get that down to ~15GB or less depending on PQ and product choices
[02:28] Priya (SE): important: dimensionality impacts both index size and compute for re-embedding (if you regenerate). Embedding generation cost scales roughly linearly with dim and model compute. so for cost+latency we often recommend 768 or 1536 depending on experiments
[02:48] Sofia (Acme): ok can you give ballpark latency numbers for generating embeddings and for rerank?
[03:00] Priya (SE): sure. using Redwood Dedicated on an A100-like GPU: embedding generation for a typical 1536-dim model at batch=128 is about 3-6ms per vector (amortized) in our bench; batch sizes smaller than 16 start to lose GPU efficiency. CPU-only is 10-50x slower depending on model and quantization. For the cross-encoder rerank (re-encoding candidate pairs) p95 depends on model size: a small cross-encoder (distil) can do topK=10 rerank in ~15-30ms p95 on an optimized GPU, a larger transformer could be 60-120ms
[03:38] Marco (SRE): note that cross-encoder uses KV cache heavily if you do autoregressive generation, but rerank is usually a bi-encoder/cross-encoder scoring pass; KV cache is more about generation caching, we want to make sure we don't confuse them. we do have continuous batching and batching windows to pack small requests into GPU batches to hit latency/cost targets
[04:00] Priya (SE): yeah good call. for rerank we typically do a forward pass per candidate, we can batch the K candidates together per request so K=10 can often be processed as a single batch of size 10 per query, but packing many queries together gives better GPU throughput — tradeoff is latency window. if you need strict 50ms p95 we recommend small batching windows + lower model size or a dedicated pool
[04:30] Dana (Acme): we care about 75ms p95 end-to-end. that includes index lookup, network, and rerank. is that realistic at 500 qps?
[04:45] Priya (SE): 75ms p95 is realistic if you: 1) keep cross-encoder small/efficient (or use distilled models), 2) run rerank on Dedicated GPUs with auto-burst disabled so you have headroom, and 3) use local index (in-memory HNSW) collocated or with low-latency NVMe. at 500 qps you probably need enough shards to keep per-shard qps moderate; e.g., 4-8 GPUs in a dedicated pool depending on model size and batching policy
[05:12] Jordan (AE): to add to cost side, we prepared a rough cost model in the spreadsheet — priya will share it — it includes cost per 1M embedding calls and cost per 1M rerank requests for a few model sizes and batching regimes
[05:28] Priya (SE): (link posted) benchmark notes: we ran synthetic 100k queries for dims 768/1536/2048; GPU batch=64/128 gave best amortized throughput. example numbers (derived from our bench so ballpark):
[05:45] Priya (SE): - 768-dim embedding gen: ~2.5ms/vector @ batch=128 GPU
[05:52] Priya (SE): - 1536-dim: ~4.5ms/vector @ batch=128 GPU
[05:58] Priya (SE): - cross-encoder rerank (small distil) topK=10: ~18ms p95 @ batch per-GPU sufficient; larger cross-encoder: ~70ms p95
[06:10] Omar (Acme): how does batching affect tail latency? we can't wait 100ms to accumulate a batch
[06:18] Priya (SE): tradeoffs: batching window sizes of 5-10ms can pack a few requests without hurting tail much. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with SLAs per route: small window for latency critical routes, longer for async heavy throughput. We can set a max batching delay of e.g., 5ms for your hot path
[06:40] Sofia (Acme): storage / index costs for 10M vectors if we quantize?
[06:47] Priya (SE): with PQ or OPQ + int8 you can get to ~10-20GB for 10M x 1536 depending on codebook. If you use HNSW with compressed vectors, memory for the graph adds overhead — plan ~1.2-1.8x index overhead on top of vector store depending on connectivity (efConstruction/M)
[07:05] Marco (SRE): on VPC/private deployments: we can deploy the index and rerank pool within your VPC so traffic never leaves your network. there are network egress patterns to be aware of; we support customer-managed KMS/HSM for keys, and audit logs streamed to your SIEM.
[07:25] Dana (Acme): great. about quantization — we heard int4 can keep quality but speed ups are model-dependent. what's Redwood's support?
[07:33] Priya (SE): Redwood runtime supports int8 and experimental int4 quantization. int8 is production-ready on Dedicated and Private; int4 can save more memory and speed but quality/regression risks are higher. our Optimize toolkit will recommend quant profiles per workload; we'd run our eval harness against your relevance tests before recommending int4 in prod
[07:55] Omar (Acme): second question: cross-encoder compute model — do you recommend running cross-encoder on GPU always or CPU for small models?
[08:05] Priya (SE): for topK=10 heavy volume, GPU typically gives better p95 and cost per request if the model isn't tiny. For very small distilled models, optimized CPU inference with AVX-512 or machine with inference accelerators (e.g., AWS Trn or Inferentia) can be competitive. But GPUs give you more headroom for spikes and easier quantization paths
[08:28] Jordan (AE): in the cost spreadsheet we show both CPU and GPU cost columns. Marco, anything to add about autoscaling for Dedicated pools?
[08:36] Marco (SRE): autoscaling is based on queue length and observed latency. for rerank we usually recommend a small reserved pool to meet SLOs plus a brief burst window. note that cold-start of new GPU nodes can add seconds, so we prefer to keep some warm nodes. also we support canary model rollout so you can test quantized variant safely
[09:02] Dana (Acme): ok let's talk numbers: what's rough cost per 1M rerank requests for a small cross-encoder on Dedicated?
[09:12] Priya (SE): ballpark: small cross-encoder on Dedicated GPU with efficient batching: $150-$400 / 1M rerank requests depending on batching and utilization. If you push to CPU-only it's higher or latency increases. Embedding generation cost per 1M vectors: for 1536-dim: ~$50-$120 depending on model and batch efficiency. these are variable; we'll supply exact numbers in the spreadsheet
[09:42] Omar (Acme): can Redwood cache rerank outputs for repeated queries?
[09:47] Priya (SE): yes, we recommend a multi-layer cache: prefix caching for frequent queries, short-term in-memory LRU for hot queries, and optional semantically-aware cache using approximate keying. that reduces compute significantly for repeated queries
[10:08] Sofia (Acme): any notes about KV cache here?
[10:11] Priya (SE): KV cache is primarily for autoregressive generation to avoid recomputing previous tokens; for cross-encoder rerank it's less applicable. However if you do sequence-to-sequence rerank or generate explanations we can leverage KV caching and warm caches per user/session
[10:30] Jordan (AE): moving to infra: acme wants private deployment in VPC with strict egress rules, can you outline the constraints and checklist?
[10:36] Marco (SRE): checklist we use: 1) VPC peering/private endpoint setup 2) Subnet/TGW routing for GPU nodes 3) KMS/HSM integration for key management 4) Audit log sink to customer SIEM 5) Egress rules (allowlist Redwood control plane endpoints) 6) Optional on-prem container pack if you need air-gap. we'll send the doc
[10:55] Dana (Acme): perfect. also curious about regression monitoring on embeddings — how do we detect quality drift after quantization or model upgrades?
[11:04] Priya (SE): Redwood Optimize integrates eval sets; we run A/B comparisons on holdout queries and report MRR/recall changes. before any rollout we run automatic evals and flag regressions; we can gate rollouts on minimal delta thresholds
[11:20] Jordan (AE): let's talk experiment plan: we'll do two legs — bench on Redwood Dedicated with your sample data, and a small Private pilot if Dedicated looks good. Priya, outline bench steps?
[11:33] Priya (SE): bench steps: 1) ingest 200k sample into index (we'll create HNSW and PQ variants), 2) precompute embeddings for dims 768/1536, 3) run 100k retrieval queries with various QPS patterns, 4) run rerank topK=10 with small and medium cross-encoders, 5) capture p50/p95/p99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, and cost metrics. We'll share the notebook and spreadsheet.
[12:01] Omar (Acme): what telemetry do you expose?
[12:05] Marco (SRE): per-route latency histograms, token-level cost breakdown, batching metrics, GPU utilization, queue lengths, and audit logs. dashboard and traces via Redwood Console; we can forward metrics into customer prometheus/grafana if wanted
[12:22] Dana (Acme): great. one last question — model variants and fallbacks; if Dedicated is saturated can requests fall back to hosted smaller model?
[12:31] Priya (SE): yes, routings can be configured by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or region-first. fallback to smaller model or region is automatic per policy. we can set strict SLOs and fallback thresholds
[12:43] Jordan (AE): next steps recap: Priya will run bench on Dedicated, Jordan will share spreadsheet, Marco sends VPC checklist, and we'll meet next week to review.
[12:52] Dana (Acme): thanks everyone, good session.

[End of transcript]
